title: Why long-term rates can rise while the Fed stands still
layers: The 10-year Treasury yield is set by investors buying and selling bonds every day, not by the Fed. It can rise even while the Fed holds its own rate steady.

A long-term yield is roughly the average short-term rate investors expect over the next ten years, plus a term premium: extra pay for locking money up through unknown inflation, government deficits and a flood of new bonds. When inflation expectations rise or the government borrows heavily, buyers demand more, bond prices fall and yields climb.
Lending for ten years is a bet on a decade of inflation and policy. When that future looks less certain, lenders want to be paid for the risk.
The Fed steers the short end of the curve; markets set the long end. Mortgages, corporate loans and stock valuations follow the long end.
What are inflation expectations doing right now?
Is government borrowing rising?
Do I need fixed-rate debt now, or can I wait?

title: Crack spreads: why diesel can soar faster than oil
layers: Nobody puts crude oil in a truck. Crude has to be refined into products like gasoline, diesel and jet fuel, and each product has its own price set by its own supply and demand. The gap between what a refinery pays for crude and what it earns selling the products is called the crack spread, because refining 'cracks' heavy oil molecules into lighter fuels. When that gap blows out, fuel prices can climb much faster than oil.

The US Energy Information Administration uses a simple model called the 3:2:1 crack spread: three barrels of crude yield roughly two barrels of gasoline and one barrel of diesel. Add the wholesale price of the two barrels of gasoline and the one of diesel (fuel is quoted per gallon, so multiply by 42 gallons per barrel), subtract the cost of three barrels of crude, and divide by three. The result is a rough profit per barrel before the refinery's other costs. Analysts also track single-product spreads. Example with made-up round numbers: if crude costs $90 a barrel and diesel sells wholesale for $4.50 a gallon, a barrel of diesel is worth $189, so the diesel crack is $99. In August 2026 the real US diesel crack passed $100 a barrel for the first time. The spread widens when refining capacity, not oil, is the bottleneck: refineries knocked out by attacks or hurricanes, plants already running flat out (US refineries hit 98% utilization in late August 2026), low inventories, or a seasonal jump in demand. Diesel demand rises in autumn with harvest and trucking (US distillate use rises about 4% from September to October on average) and then winter heating oil, while gasoline enters its slow season. That is why diesel can set records while gasoline barely moves.

Refineries are huge, slow to build and few in number, so a fuel shortage cannot be fixed by pumping more crude. In 2022, when Russia's invasion of Ukraine disrupted one of the world's biggest diesel exporters, US diesel hit a weekly high of $5.81 a gallon. In 2026 the same thing is happening for a different mix of reasons: attacks on Russian refineries cut its diesel output about 30%, and the Iran war choked flows through the Strait of Hormuz. Diesel matters more to the economy than gasoline because it moves freight, food and machinery, so a diesel squeeze spreads into prices of almost everything that gets shipped. Wide crack spreads move money too: they are a windfall for refiners and a cost for airlines, truckers, farmers and retailers.

Oil is the raw material, but the price you and your suppliers pay is set at the refinery. When product prices rise faster than crude, the problem is refining capacity, and it usually takes longer to fix than a crude shortage.
Is the price jump in crude itself, or in refined products like diesel?
Who in my supply chain pays for fuel, and how quickly do they pass it on to me?
What would ease the bottleneck: new refining capacity, restored exports, or the end of a seasonal peak?

title: Cyclical industries: when record profits are a warning
layers: A cyclical industry is one where profits rise and fall in big waves, because prices swing with the balance of supply and demand rather than with anything the company controls. Memory chips, oil, steel, shipping, airlines, chemicals and homebuilding all behave this way. What they share: the product is close to a commodity (one maker's chip or barrel is nearly interchangeable with another's), buyers shop on price, and new capacity is expensive and takes years to build. Micron, one of three big memory makers, shows the pattern. In fiscal 2022 it earned $8.7 billion. In fiscal 2023 revenue fell 49% and it lost $5.8 billion, with a gross margin of minus 9.1%, meaning it sold chips for less than they cost to make. By mid-2026 its adjusted gross margin had reached 87%.

The cycle runs like a loop. Demand jumps (in 2026, AI data centers need huge amounts of memory) while supply is fixed, so prices soar. Soaring prices create fat profits, and every producer uses them to build new factories. Factories take two to three years to come online, so they tend to arrive together, often just as demand cools. Now supply outruns demand, buyers stop ordering and burn through their stockpiles, and prices fall fast because a factory that has already been built is cheapest to keep running, even at a thin margin. That is what happened in early 2023: Micron's DRAM prices dropped about 20% in a single quarter, revenue fell 53% from a year earlier, it wrote down $1.43 billion of inventory and planned to cut close to 15% of its workforce. Losses then force producers to cut investment, supply tightens, and the next boom starts. A second force is technology. A cheaper way to make the same product, like a denser chip design that fits more memory in the same space, works like new supply even before a new factory opens, because it lowers what each unit costs to produce.

Cyclicals trick investors in a specific way. The price-to-earnings ratio (share price divided by profit per share) usually signals 'cheap' when it is low. For a cyclical company at the top of the cycle, profits are temporarily huge, so the P/E looks low exactly when the risk is highest. At the bottom, profits are tiny or negative, so the P/E looks high or meaningless just when the outlook is about to improve. Professional investors handle this by looking at 'normalized' or 'mid-cycle' earnings, an average across a full boom and bust, and by watching supply rather than demand: how much capacity competitors are building, how full customer inventories are, and whether a new low-cost producer is entering. Markets also move ahead of profits. On October 12–13, 2026, memory stocks fell sharply on news that China's CXMT might make denser chips, even though prices were still rising and the threat was not yet in production. Micron's own earlier cycle shows how fast profits fade: from a $14.1 billion peak in fiscal 2018, net income fell 81% in two years.

In a commodity business, the most dangerous moment is when everyone is earning record profits, because those profits fund the new supply that ends them. Judge a cyclical company by its earnings across a full cycle, and watch the supply side more closely than the demand story.
Is this company's product easy to swap for a competitor's, so that price decides who wins?
Are today's profits far above the company's average over the last full cycle?
How much new capacity are competitors building, and when does it come online?
If prices fell 20% in a quarter, could this company still cover its costs and debts?
